title: Metal-Carbon Bonds and Hapticity
description: Sigma, pi, alkyl, carbene — and the eta-notation that names them

concepts.title: Classifying M-C Bonds
concepts.contentHtml:
Organometallic chemistry is the chemistry of compounds containing at least one metal-carbon bond. The M-C bond can be highly ionic (organolithiums, Grignards: C δ-, M δ+) or strongly covalent (Pt, Pd, Rh organyls). Where the bond falls on this spectrum dictates reactivity: ionic species are nucleophilic at carbon, covalent species participate in well-defined catalytic cycles.

Ligand classes by donor type. Sigma-donors: alkyls (M-CH3), aryls (M-C6H5), hydrides. Pi-donors and pi-acceptors: carbonyls (M-CO is the canonical pi-acceptor — back-donation from filled metal d into CO pi*), olefins, dienes, arenes. Carbenes (M=CR2) split into Fischer (electrophilic, low oxidation state, pi-acceptor heteroatom) and Schrock (nucleophilic, high oxidation state, alkylidene). Carbynes have a metal-carbon triple bond (M≡CR).

The bonding picture matters because back-donation tunes everything: CO stretching frequencies in IR drop as electron-rich metals push more density into CO pi*, and that same back-donation activates substrates toward nucleophilic attack. Reading nu(CO) in cm^-1 is reading the electron density of the metal.

concepts.title: Hapticity and the Eta Notation
concepts.contentHtml:
Hapticity describes how many contiguous atoms of a ligand bond to the metal, written with the Greek letter eta (η). An η^1-allyl bonds through one carbon; an η^3-allyl uses all three carbons of the C3 unit. Cyclopentadienyl can be η^1 (sigma-bonded, one C) or η^5 (pentahapto, sandwich-style).

Ferrocene, Fe(η^5-C5H5)2, has both Cp rings bound through all five carbons — the iconic 1951 sandwich structure that launched the field. Dibenzenechromium uses η^6 arenes. The famous 'ring slip' phenomenon (η^5 → η^3 → η^1) lets a coordinatively saturated metal open a coordination site for a new ligand without ejecting Cp entirely.

Hapticity is more than notation: it controls electron count. An η^5-Cp donates five electrons (covalent counting) or six (ionic counting, as Cp^-). When you change hapticity, you change the number of electrons the metal sees. That's how a stable 18-electron complex transiently becomes a reactive 16-electron species — slip the Cp, open a site, bind a substrate, slip it back.
mathExpressions: \eta^n: n = \text{number of contiguous atoms bonded to M}

concepts.title: Covalent vs Ionic Electron Counting
concepts.contentHtml:
Organometallic chemists count electrons two ways and the answer (the total) must agree, but the bookkeeping differs.

Covalent (neutral) method: every ligand is treated as neutral; a halide is X• (1 electron donor), a hydride H• (1 e), CO is :CO (2 e), Cp• (5 e), η^2-alkene (2 e). The metal contributes its group-number electrons (Fe: 8, Pd: 10). For Cp2Fe: Fe(0) gives 8, two Cp give 10, total = 18. Ionic method: ligands are treated as charged. Cp^- (6 e), H^- (2 e), Cl^- (2 e). Metal oxidation state is set first; remaining d-electrons + ligand pairs count. For Cp2Fe: Fe(II) = d^6, two Cp^- = 12, total = 18. Same answer.

The 18-electron rule: stable diamagnetic transition metal complexes tend to have 18 valence electrons, mirroring the noble gas configuration (n)s^2 (n)p^6 (n)d^10. Exceptions are common: square-planar d^8 (Pt(II), Pd(II), Rh(I), Ir(I)) prefers 16 electrons because a fifth ligand would have to occupy a high-energy d_{x^2-y^2}-derived orbital. Many catalytic intermediates are 16-electron — the 'open site' is what makes them reactive.
mathExpressions: \text{EAN (effective atomic number)} = d_{\text{metal}} + \sum (\text{electrons donated by ligands})

title: Elementary Steps of Catalysis
description: Oxidative addition, reductive elimination, insertion, beta-hydride

concepts.title: Oxidative Addition and Reductive Elimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Catalysis is a sequence of elementary steps; you cannot understand a cycle without naming them. Oxidative addition (OA): a metal inserts into an X-Y bond, raising its oxidation state by 2 and its coordination number by 2. Pd(0) + Ph-Br → Pd(II)(Ph)(Br). The metal pays two electrons to break X-Y and form M-X and M-Y bonds. OA is favored for electron-rich, low-oxidation-state, coordinatively unsaturated metals (Pd(0), Ni(0), Pt(0), Ir(I)).

Reductive elimination (RE): the reverse. Two cis ligands on the metal couple, freeing M and lowering its oxidation state by 2. Pd(II)(R)(R') → Pd(0) + R-R'. RE drives the product-forming step in cross-coupling. It demands the two coupling groups sit cis; trans complexes have to isomerize first.

Mechanism varies. OA of nonpolar bonds (H-H, C-H) often goes through a three-centered concerted transition state. OA of polar C-X bonds can be concerted, SN2-like (with backside attack and inversion at carbon), or radical. Tracking which mechanism operates explains stereochemistry, rates, and selectivity for a given substrate-catalyst pair.

concepts.title: Migratory Insertion and Beta-Hydride Elimination
concepts.contentHtml:
Migratory insertion: a sigma-bonded ligand (alkyl, hydride) migrates onto a cis pi-bonded ligand (alkene, CO). M(R)(CO) → M(C(O)R): the alkyl migrates to coordinated CO, forming an acyl. M(H)(CH2=CHR) → M(CH2-CH2R): a hydride migrates to a coordinated alkene, forming an alkyl. The C-C or C-H bond is made within the coordination sphere; an open site appears where the migrating group came from.

Beta-hydride elimination: the reverse. A metal alkyl with a hydrogen on the carbon beta to the metal can transfer that H to the metal, producing a coordinated alkene and a metal hydride. M-CH2-CH2R → M(H)(CH2=CHR). Beta-H elimination requires (i) an H on Cβ, (ii) a vacant coordination site cis to the alkyl, and (iii) a syn-periplanar M-C-C-H geometry.

Beta-H elimination is everywhere: it is what kills many late-metal alkyls before they can do useful chemistry, but it is also the chain-transfer step in olefin polymerization and the productive step in dehydrogenations and the Heck reaction. Suppress it (no beta-H, blocked geometry, electron-poor metal) and you can make stable alkyls; encourage it and you make olefins. Modern Pd cross-coupling depends on aryl groups, which have no beta-H, sidestepping the problem entirely.

concepts.title: Sigma-Bond Metathesis and Transmetalation
concepts.contentHtml:
Sigma-bond metathesis: a four-centered concerted exchange between an M-X bond and a Y-Z bond, going M-X + Y-Z → M-Y + X-Z without changing the metal's oxidation state. Common for d^0 early metals (Sc, Y, Ti, Zr, lanthanides) which cannot do oxidative addition because they have no d-electrons to spare. The transition state is a planar four-membered ring with simultaneous bond-making and bond-breaking.

Transmetalation: an organic group migrates from one metal to another, M-R + M'-X → M-X + M'-R. It is the productive step in Suzuki coupling (boronate transfers an aryl to Pd), Negishi coupling (organozinc to Pd), Stille coupling (organotin to Pd), and Sonogashira (acetylide from Cu to Pd). Each variant differs in the activator and in functional-group tolerance.

The unifying picture: metal centers shuffle organic groups around using a small alphabet of elementary steps. A catalytic cycle is just a sequence — for a Suzuki coupling, that sequence is OA, transmetalation, RE — and identifying which step is rate-limiting is the first move in optimizing or troubleshooting a reaction.
mathExpressions: \sigma\text{-bond metathesis: } M\text{-}X + Y\text{-}Z \to M\text{-}Y + X\text{-}Z, \quad \Delta(\text{ox. state}) = 0

title: Hydrogenation: Wilkinson, Crabtree, Noyori
description: From racemic H2 addition to billion-dollar asymmetric catalysis

concepts.title: Wilkinson's Catalyst
concepts.contentHtml:
Wilkinson's catalyst, RhCl(PPh3)3, was reported by Geoffrey Wilkinson in 1965 and remains the textbook homogeneous hydrogenation catalyst. The cycle: dissociate one PPh3 to make a 14-electron RhCl(PPh3)2 active species, oxidatively add H2 to give a Rh(III) dihydride, coordinate the alkene, migratory-insert one hydride to make a Rh(III) alkyl, and reductively eliminate the alkane while regenerating Rh(I).

It hydrogenates terminal and disubstituted alkenes well but stalls on tetrasubstituted alkenes (steric crowding around Rh). It tolerates many functional groups (esters, ketones, amines, halides) — a major contrast to heterogeneous Pd/C, which can over-reduce. The catalyst is sensitive to oxygen and to coordinating impurities that displace PPh3 from the active site.

Wilkinson's complex earned its 1973 Nobel along with ferrocene and changed industrial hydrogenation. It established the now-ubiquitous mental model: a homogeneous transition-metal catalyst is a coordination complex that runs through OA, insertion, RE in a closed cycle, and a chemist's job is to tune the ligands to control rate and selectivity.

concepts.title: Crabtree's Catalyst
concepts.contentHtml:
Crabtree's catalyst, [Ir(cod)(PCy3)(py)][PF6], reported by Robert Crabtree in 1977, is the go-to for hindered alkenes. It hydrogenates tri- and tetrasubstituted alkenes that defeat Wilkinson's catalyst — far higher rates per turnover. The ionic Ir(I) center plus the bulky tricyclohexylphosphine and pyridine ligands create a uniquely active system in non-coordinating solvents like dichloromethane.

Crabtree's catalyst pioneered directed hydrogenation: a polar functional group (hydroxyl, amide, ester) on the substrate coordinates to Ir and steers H2 delivery to the same face. The result is high diastereoselectivity controlled by substrate geometry rather than ligand chirality. Stork and Crabtree showed >99:1 diastereomeric ratios on rigid steroidal substrates this way.

The downside: in coordinating solvents (alcohols, ethers), donor solvent molecules outcompete the substrate-directing group and selectivity collapses. Substrates and conditions must be matched. Crabtree's work also catalyzed (literally and figuratively) the rise of cationic late-metal catalysts: the lesson that an open coordination site, not just an electron-rich metal, drives reactivity.

concepts.title: Asymmetric Hydrogenation: Noyori and BINAP
concepts.contentHtml:
Asymmetric catalysis: a chiral catalyst converts a prochiral substrate into a single enantiomer. Even tiny ee (enantiomeric excess) advantages multiply by turnover number — one chiral catalyst can produce gigamoles of single-enantiomer drug.

Ryoji Noyori's BINAP ligand (2,2'-bis(diphenylphosphino)-1,1'-binaphthyl), reported in 1980, locks Ru or Rh into a chiral pocket. Ru(BINAP)(OAc)2 hydrogenates beta-keto esters with >99% ee — the basis for the industrial synthesis of (S)-naproxen, levofloxacin, and many fragrances. Knowles' DIPAMP-Rh achieved the L-DOPA synthesis (Parkinson's drug) at Monsanto in the 1970s, the first commercial asymmetric catalysis. The shared 2001 Nobel went to Knowles, Noyori, and Sharpless for asymmetric catalysis.

Mechanistic insight matters: Noyori's later Ru-(BINAP)(diamine) catalysts hydrogenate ketones (not just alkenes) via a metal-ligand bifunctional outer-sphere mechanism — the substrate never coordinates to Ru directly. The N-H on the amine ligand and the M-H deliver across a six-membered transition state. The take-home: ligand design encodes both rate and stereochemistry; once you understand the transition state, you design the ligand.

title: Industrial CO and O2 Catalysis
description: Hydroformylation, the Wacker process, and selectivity at scale

concepts.title: Hydroformylation: The Oxo Process
concepts.contentHtml:
Hydroformylation (the oxo process) adds H and CHO across an alkene to make an aldehyde: RCH=CH2 + H2 + CO → RCH2CH2CHO (linear) + RCH(CHO)CH3 (branched). Discovered by Otto Roelen at Ruhrchemie in 1938, it now produces over 10 million tonnes of aldehydes per year — feedstocks for plasticizers (di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate), detergents, and solvents.

Cycle: a coordinatively unsaturated HM(CO)n binds the alkene, migratory-inserts to a metal alkyl, coordinates CO, migratory-inserts again to a metal acyl, oxidatively adds H2, and reductively eliminates the aldehyde while regenerating HM(CO)n. The original cobalt catalyst HCo(CO)4 needed 200-300 bar CO pressure and 150 °C; modern rhodium-phosphine catalysts (Rh-TPPTS in the Ruhrchemie/Rhone-Poulenc biphasic process) work at 50 bar and 120 °C.

Linear-to-branched (l/b) ratio matters: linear aldehydes make better plasticizers and detergents. Bulky bidentate phosphines (BIPHEPHOS, XANTPHOS) push l/b ratios to >30:1 by sterically disfavoring the branched insertion. The story is a textbook of ligand-controlled regioselectivity.

concepts.title: Wacker Oxidation
concepts.contentHtml:
The Wacker process oxidizes ethylene to acetaldehyde with PdCl2/CuCl2 in aqueous HCl: CH2=CH2 + 1/2 O2 → CH3CHO. Industrialized by Wacker-Chemie in 1959, it once supplied a large fraction of world acetaldehyde demand, though demand has since shifted as acetaldehyde-derived markets have shrunk.

Mechanism: Pd(II) coordinates ethylene, water attacks the bound olefin (anti hydroxypalladation), beta-H elimination forms a Pd(II) vinyl alcohol, isomerization gives Pd(0) + acetaldehyde. Pd(0) is reoxidized to Pd(II) by Cu(II); the resulting Cu(I) is reoxidized by O2. The Pd-Cu redox couple is what makes the cycle catalytic in both metals — without it, you would need stoichiometric oxidant.

The Wacker reaction generalizes: terminal alkenes give methyl ketones (Markovnikov regioselectivity, the Tsuji-Wacker reaction is widely used in fine-chemical synthesis). Internal alkenes are sluggish. The combination of Pd(II) electrophilic activation + nucleophilic water attack is also the template for many later Pd(II)-catalyzed C-H and C-O bond-forming processes — Wacker is in some sense the prototype for modern Pd(II) oxidation chemistry.

concepts.title: Monsanto and Cativa: Acetic Acid
concepts.contentHtml:
Acetic acid is made industrially by carbonylating methanol: CH3OH + CO → CH3COOH. The Monsanto process (1970) used [Rh(CO)2I2]^- with HI promoter; the rate-determining step is oxidative addition of CH3I to the Rh(I) anion. This single reaction supplied roughly half the world's acetic acid for decades.

BP's Cativa process (1996) replaced rhodium with iridium, [Ir(CO)2I2]^-, with a Ru promoter. Cativa runs at lower water concentration, gives higher selectivity, suppresses side products, and is more energy-efficient. Iridium oxidatively adds CH3I about 150 times faster than rhodium does — a large mechanistic gap that motivates the metal switch.

Both processes are textbook 'simple' cycles — OA, migratory CO insertion, RE — yet hide subtle competitions between methyl iodide activation, water-gas shift, hydrolysis of the iodide promoter, and the recycled CO partial pressure. The shift from Rh to Ir is one of the rare cases where a real industrial process changed metals because mechanism understanding showed Ir would do better. It is what mechanistic chemistry looks like at gigatonne scale.

title: Pd Cross-Coupling
description: Suzuki, Negishi, Stille, Heck — and the 2010 Nobel

concepts.title: The Cross-Coupling Family
concepts.contentHtml:
Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling joins two carbon fragments through a Pd(0)/Pd(II) cycle: oxidative addition of an electrophile (Ar-X), transmetalation with a nucleophilic organometallic, and reductive elimination of the new C-C bond. The variants differ only in the nucleophile and the activator that primes it for transmetalation.

Suzuki-Miyaura (1979): organoboron (boronic acid, boronate ester) + aqueous base. Air-stable, water-tolerant, low toxicity — the most-used C-C bond-forming reaction in pharma. Negishi (1977): organozinc, very fast and highly chemoselective for aryl-alkyl bonds. Stille (1977): organotin, broad scope but the tin byproducts are toxic and hard to remove. Sonogashira: terminal alkyne + Cu(I) co-catalyst, the workhorse for installing alkynes. Kumada (1972): Grignard, the first cross-coupling reported, but limited functional-group tolerance.

The 2010 Nobel went to Heck, Negishi, and Suzuki — recognition that this family of reactions transformed pharmaceutical and materials synthesis. A typical analysis suggests most modern drug candidates contain at least one bond made by Pd cross-coupling. The reaction democratized aryl-aryl, aryl-vinyl, and aryl-alkyl bond formation, replacing a generation of multistep classical methods (lithium-halogen exchange, Ullmann couplings) with a single mild step.

concepts.title: The Heck and Buchwald-Hartwig Reactions
concepts.contentHtml:
The Heck reaction couples an aryl/vinyl halide with an alkene to install a new vinyl group: Ar-X + CH2=CHR → Ar-CH=CHR. The mechanism differs from the others: after oxidative addition, the alkene coordinates to Pd, migratory-inserts (carbopalladation), then beta-H eliminates to release the alkene product and a Pd(II)-H, which loses HX to regenerate Pd(0). No transmetalation step. The Heck is regio- and stereo-selective: the new C-C bond forms at the less-substituted end of the alkene with overall trans (E) geometry, because the syn migratory insertion and syn beta-H elimination steps work in concert.

The Buchwald-Hartwig amination (mid-1990s) extends Pd cross-coupling to nitrogen nucleophiles: Ar-X + HNR2 → Ar-NR2. It made aryl C-N bond formation routine, replacing classical Ullmann couplings that required stoichiometric copper at 200 °C. Buchwald's bulky biaryl phosphines (SPhos, XPhos, RuPhos, BrettPhos) and Hartwig's ferrocene-based ligands (DPPF, JosiPhos) were essential — they accelerate both oxidative addition (electron-rich Pd) and reductive elimination (steric pressure).

Buchwald-Hartwig is now ubiquitous in pharma: most drug candidates with aryl amines (a huge fraction of the medicinal chemistry palette) use it. The reaction is so reliable that the limiting factor in drug-target diversity is often what Buchwald-Hartwig conditions can be made to tolerate.

concepts.title: Ligands: Phosphines and NHCs
concepts.contentHtml:
The same metal can do wildly different things depending on its ligand. Pd cross-coupling lives or dies by phosphine choice. Tolman's cone angle (steric size in degrees) and electronic parameter (chi, calibrated against nu(CO) of Ni(CO)3L) provide the steric-electronic axes for ligand design. PPh3 (cone 145°, mildly donating) is the workhorse but slow on aryl chlorides. P(t-Bu)3 (cone 182°, strongly donating) accelerates oxidative addition of Ar-Cl 100-1000-fold and forces RE through steric pressure.

Buchwald's biaryl phosphines (SPhos, XPhos) combine a bulky dialkylphosphine with a neighboring aryl ring that weakly coordinates to Pd to stabilize the active monoligated 12-electron Pd(0). They are at the heart of room-temperature aryl chloride coupling — a reaction that needed 130 °C with PPh3.

N-heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs), popularized by Arduengo (1991) for free, isolable species and by Herrmann/Nolan as catalyst ligands, are even stronger sigma-donors than phosphines and form thermally robust M-C(NHC) bonds. IMes, IPr, SIMes have replaced phosphines in many high-performance coupling and metathesis catalysts. NHC complexes are typically air-stable, easy to handle, and recyclable — important for industrial process chemistry.

title: Olefin Metathesis
description: Grubbs, Schrock, and the Chauvin mechanism that won 2005

concepts.title: The Chauvin Mechanism
concepts.contentHtml:
Olefin metathesis swaps the carbene halves of two alkenes: 2 RCH=CHR' becomes RCH=CHR + R'CH=CHR'. It looks like magic until you see the mechanism. Yves Chauvin proposed in 1971 that the active species is a metal carbene (M=CHR) and the cycle goes through a metallacyclobutane intermediate. Cycle: M=CHR + CH2=CHR' coordinate, [2+2] cycloaddition gives a four-membered M(CHR)(CHR')CH2 metallacyclobutane, retro-[2+2] gives M=CHR' + CH2=CHR (productive) or back to starting materials (degenerate).

For decades the mechanism was disputed because metal carbenes seemed exotic. Tebbe's reagent (Cp2Ti(μ-CH2)(μ-Cl)AlMe2, 1978) and Schrock's well-defined alkylidenes (Mo, W, Re) made the carbene intermediate observable, putting Chauvin's proposal beyond doubt.

Equilibrium: metathesis is freely reversible, so productive selectivity comes from removing one product (usually ethylene gas) by Le Chatelier. The reaction is the basis of ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), ring-closing metathesis (RCM) — a star reaction in macrocyclic drug synthesis — and cross metathesis. The 2005 Nobel went to Chauvin, Schrock, and Grubbs.

concepts.title: Schrock and Grubbs Catalysts
concepts.contentHtml:
Schrock catalysts are high-oxidation-state alkylidenes of Mo or W with bulky imido and alkoxide ligands, e.g. Mo(=N-Ar)(=CHCMe2Ph)(OR)2. They are extremely active and tolerate hindered substrates, but they are oxygen- and water-sensitive (high-OS d^0 metals love water and won't share with substrates). Schrock catalysts are made and used under glovebox conditions and were until the 1990s the only choice for demanding metatheses.

Grubbs catalysts are low-oxidation-state Ru alkylidenes. Grubbs I (RuCl2(=CHPh)(PCy3)2, 1995) is air-stable, tolerates alcohols, water, and many functional groups, and made metathesis a routine bench reaction. Grubbs II (replaces one PCy3 with an NHC, IMesH2 / SIMes) is faster and more active toward hindered substrates. Hoveyda-Grubbs II (chelating styrenyl ether replaces the second PCy3) is recoverable and is the most-used catalyst in pharmaceutical RCM.

The trade-off summarizes the field: Schrock = activity; Grubbs = tolerance. Grubbs's instinct that ruthenium would tolerate water proved transformative. The drug Vaniqa (eflornithine), the macrocyclic HCV protease inhibitors (simeprevir, grazoprevir), and many natural-product total syntheses depend on Grubbs catalysts.

concepts.title: Selectivity: Z-Selective and Stereoretentive
concepts.contentHtml:
Most metathesis catalysts give the thermodynamic E-isomer (trans alkene) because the metallacyclobutane intermediate prefers the less-strained all-trans geometry. For many natural products, the cis (Z) isomer is the desired target. Until 2011, accessing Z-alkenes by metathesis was nearly impossible.

Z-selective catalysts: Grubbs and Hoveyda independently designed second-generation Ru catalysts with bulky chelating dithiolate (Hoveyda) or pivalate (Grubbs) ligands that force the metallacyclobutane into a cis-disposed geometry. The result is alkenes with >95% Z selectivity in many substrates. Hoveyda's group and Grubbs's group pushed this through to the gram scale for natural-product targets like the insect pheromones and prostaglandins.

More recent stereoretentive metathesis takes a Z-alkene to a different Z-alkene without scrambling — useful when the substrate already has Z-stereochemistry that must be preserved. The general lesson: the metallacyclobutane intermediate is the chiral pocket of metathesis, and engineering its substituent pattern engineers product geometry. As of 2024, Z-selective and even E,Z-selective catalysts are commercial products from Materia and Umicore, and used in industrial fine-chemical synthesis.

title: C-H Activation and Photoredox Catalysis
description: Funcionalizing the unfunctionalized — Pd, Rh, Ir, Ru and visible light

concepts.title: Directed C-H Activation
concepts.contentHtml:
C-H activation turns an inert C-H bond into a C-M bond that can then be functionalized. Classical synthesis avoids C-H bonds because they are non-polar, ubiquitous, and similar in BDE; selectivity is the central problem. The breakthrough was directed C-H activation: a coordinating group on the substrate (pyridine, oxime, amide) binds the metal first, geometrically positioning it next to a specific C-H bond.

Mechanism varies by metal. Concerted metalation-deprotonation (CMD) is the dominant mode for Pd(II) and Ru(II) with carboxylate co-catalysts: the carboxylate plucks the proton at the same time as the M-C bond forms, in a six-membered transition state. Sigma-bond metathesis dominates for d^0 early metals. Rh and Ir often go through oxidative addition.

Pd(II)/Pd(IV) and Pd(II)/Pd(0) cycles, pioneered by Sanford, Yu, and Engle, now functionalize ortho, meta, and even remote C-H bonds with high regio- and stereo-control. The Yu group's Pd-catalyzed beta-C(sp3)-H arylation, using monoprotected amino acid (MPAA) ligands, has functionalized previously untouchable methyl groups in drug substrates and reduced multistep syntheses to single steps.
mathExpressions: \text{CMD: simultaneous M-C formation and O-H formation, six-membered TS}

concepts.title: Why C-H Activation Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
The sustainability case is direct. A traditional cross-coupling needs a pre-functionalized aryl halide; making that halide takes steps, generates halide waste, and limits which positions are accessible. C-H activation skips that whole prelude — the C-H bond is already on the substrate. Atom economy goes up, step count goes down, hazardous reagents go out. Process mass intensity (PMI), an industry metric for total mass per kg of product, drops substantially.

Selective late-stage C-H functionalization of complex molecules is the dream: take an advanced intermediate, install fluorine or methyl or aryl at one specific position, no protecting groups. The Davies, Doyle, and Du Bois groups have built a Rh-catalyzed C-H insertion toolkit (carbenoids and nitrenoids) that does this on natural-product scaffolds. Bristol-Myers Squibb has integrated C-H activation into commercial drug synthesis routes.

The frontier: undirected C-H activation, where there is no coordinating handle on the substrate. Hartwig's Ir-catalyzed C-H borylation (with B2pin2) is the leading example: it gives a boronate that can be used in any subsequent Suzuki coupling, and it is selective for the least-hindered C-H. Combining undirected borylation with Suzuki gives 'C-H functionalization by proxy' — the most general C-H method to date in industrial use.
mathExpressions: \text{PMI} = \frac{\text{total mass input}}{\text{mass of product}} \quad \text{lower is better}

concepts.title: Photoredox: Single-Electron Catalysis with Light
concepts.contentHtml:
Photoredox catalysis uses a visible-light-absorbing transition-metal complex to generate excited states that transfer single electrons to or from a substrate. Common photocatalysts are Ru(bpy)3^2+ and Ir(ppy)3 (and their fluorinated cousins): they absorb a blue/green photon, populate a long-lived metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) triplet state, and become simultaneously a stronger oxidant and a stronger reductant than the ground state.

The 2008 papers by MacMillan, Yoon, and Stephenson reignited the field. Photoredox has since enabled radical alpha-arylation, decarboxylative couplings, atom-transfer radical additions, and metallaphotoredox catalysis (combining a photocatalyst with a Ni or Pd cross-coupling cycle). Many transformations that classical two-electron chemistry could not access — coupling alkyl carboxylic acids directly to aryl halides, for instance — now run at room temperature with blue LEDs.

Kinetics: excited-state lifetimes are typically hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds, and reaction rates with substrates follow Stern-Volmer kinetics. The Stern-Volmer plot (1/τ vs. quencher concentration) measures the rate constant of single-electron transfer to a substrate, which is what mechanism people use to identify the productive step. Photoredox is now in industrial pharmaceutical research at every major company.

title: Earth-Abundant Catalysis
description: Replacing Pd, Rh, Ir with Fe, Co, Ni, Cu

concepts.title: The Cost and Toxicity Drivers
concepts.contentHtml:
Why replace precious metals at all? Cost, supply, and toxicity. Rhodium has spiked above 20,000 USD per troy ounce; iridium and palladium follow. Precious-metal residues in pharmaceutical APIs are limited to the parts-per-million range by ICH guidelines (typically <10 ppm Pd, <5 ppm Ir/Rh), forcing expensive scavenging steps. Mining footprint is large: a ton of Pd ore yields grams of metal.

Earth-abundant metals — Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Mn — are 10^4 to 10^6 times more abundant than the precious metals and orders of magnitude cheaper. Their toxicity profiles are also gentler (Fe and Cu are biological essential elements; Ni and Co are tolerated at higher residual levels in pharma). The challenge is mechanistic: Fe and Co naturally cycle through one-electron pathways (radical chemistry) rather than the clean two-electron OA/RE cycles that Pd and Ir excel at. Selectivity has historically been worse.

The decade after 2010 was a Renaissance for earth-abundant catalysis: high-spin Fe(II)/Fe(IV) and Co(I)/Co(III) cycles with redox-active ligands have closed much of the selectivity gap. Industry is paying attention because the economics are real.

concepts.title: Iron and Cobalt Catalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Iron catalysis for cross-coupling was pioneered by Kochi in the 1970s and reinvigorated by Furstner, Bedford, and Nakamura. FeCl3 plus a Grignard or ArMgBr does Kumada-type coupling at low temperature. Iron-catalyzed hydrogenation (Chirik's bis(imino)pyridine Fe complexes, Milstein's Fe pincer hydrogenations of esters and amides) has matched precious-metal performance on many substrates, sometimes with redox-active ligands that store one of the two electrons that the metal cannot.

Cobalt catalysis: Co-mediated hydroformylation predates the Rh process and is still used at scale (oxo plant cobalt catalysts work at higher pressure but are cheaper). Co pincer complexes (Hanson, Chirik) hydrogenate ketones and alkenes with high turnover. Cobaloxime (a vitamin B12 mimic) catalyzes proton reduction to H2 — a leading earth-abundant water-splitting catalyst.

Mechanistic theme: redox-active ligands (bis(imino)pyridines, alpha-diimines, pyridyl-amido) accept and release one electron, letting the metal effectively do two-electron chemistry. This is biological inspiration: vitamin B12 (cobalamin) does radical chemistry through a Co-C bond and Co(I)/Co(III) cycling. Modern earth-abundant catalysts are engineered to do the same.

concepts.title: Nickel and Copper Catalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Nickel catalysis is Pd's lighter, cheaper, and more reactive cousin. Ni(0) does oxidative addition of aryl chlorides and even aryl ethers and aryl C-O bonds — substrates Pd struggles with. The trade-off: Ni readily accesses Ni(I) and Ni(III) one-electron states, opening radical pathways that complicate selectivity. The metallaphotoredox catalysis revolution (Doyle, MacMillan, Molander) deliberately exploits Ni's radical reactivity to couple alkyl carboxylic acids, alkyl bromides, and even alkyl sulfides directly to aryl halides.

Copper catalysis is the workhorse for C-N, C-O, and C-S bond formation, especially since the Buchwald and Liu groups showed that simple Cu(I) plus an amino acid or beta-diketonate ligand replicates many Buchwald-Hartwig conditions at a fraction of the cost. Copper also catalyzes Glaser/Eglinton couplings (alkyne-alkyne homocoupling), the Chan-Lam coupling (boronic acid + amine, oxidative), and click chemistry (Cu-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition, CuAAC, Sharpless's 2022 second Nobel).

The full picture: a complete catalytic toolkit increasingly does not need precious metals. For most C-N bond formations, a copper catalyst now suffices; for many C-C couplings, nickel; for hydrogenations, iron or cobalt. The shift will accelerate as supply pressure on precious metals tightens.

title: Mechanism Tools: Kinetics, KIE, Hammett, DFT
description: How chemists prove a catalytic cycle, not just propose one

concepts.title: Rate Laws and the Resting State
concepts.contentHtml:
Mechanism is not asserted, it is supported by data. The first move is to measure the rate law. If rate = k[cat][ArX][R-B] in a Suzuki reaction, all three are involved before the rate-determining step (RDS); if rate is independent of [R-B], transmetalation is fast (post-RDS) and OA is rate-limiting.

The resting state of a catalyst is the form in which the metal spends most of its time during turnover — usually pre-RDS in the cycle. Identifying it (by NMR, IR, or in situ X-ray under reaction conditions) tells you which step is slow and where to push experimentally. If the resting state is Pd(II)-Ar (post-OA, pre-transmetalation), increasing the boronate concentration helps; if it is Pd(0)-L2 (pre-OA), changing the ligand or substrate helps.

The Eyring equation connects rate constants to activation parameters: k = (k_B T / h) exp(-ΔG‡ / RT). Plotting ln(k/T) vs 1/T gives ΔH‡ (slope) and ΔS‡ (intercept), the activation enthalpy and entropy. Large negative ΔS‡ implies an associative or highly ordered transition state; near-zero ΔS‡ implies a dissociative or unimolecular step. These numbers constrain mechanism quantitatively.
mathExpressions: k = \frac{k_B T}{h} \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G^{\ddagger}}{RT}\right) = \frac{k_B T}{h} \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S^{\ddagger}}{R}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H^{\ddagger}}{RT}\right)

concepts.title: KIE, Hammett, and Linear Free Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
The kinetic isotope effect (KIE): replacing an H with a D in the substrate slows the reaction if the C-H bond is broken in or before the RDS. A primary KIE (kH/kD between 2 and 7 at room temperature) signals direct C-H bond cleavage. A small KIE (<1.5) suggests the C-H bond is intact through the RDS. KIEs are the most direct mechanistic probe in C-H activation.

The Hammett equation: log(k_X/k_H) = ρ σ_X. Substituting different X groups on a phenyl ring of the substrate changes the rate. Sigma_X (Hammett substituent constant) is fixed; ρ (the reaction constant, the slope of log k vs sigma) depends on the reaction. Large positive ρ (>1) means buildup of negative charge near the substituent in the transition state — nucleophilic attack on the aromatic ring, for instance. Negative ρ means buildup of positive charge.

For Pd-catalyzed OA of Ar-Br, ρ is typically positive (electron-poor Ar adds faster) — the Pd inserts into a more electrophilic C-Br bond more readily. For C-H activation by CMD, ρ is also positive, consistent with a partially anionic carbon in the TS. Each ρ value is a quantitative fingerprint of charge distribution at the transition state.

concepts.title: Computational Catalysis: DFT Energy Profiles
concepts.contentHtml:
Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculates the electronic structure of organometallic species and the energies of transition states. A modern paper proposing a new catalytic cycle almost always pairs experiment with a DFT energy profile: ground-state intermediate I_1, transition state TS_1 with relative ΔG‡, intermediate I_2, and so on along the cycle.

Common functionals for transition metals: B3LYP (older, fast), M06 and M06-L (Truhlar, parametrized for organometallics), wB97X-D (long-range corrected, includes dispersion). Dispersion corrections (D3, D4) matter enormously for bulky ligands — without them, a SPhos-Pd complex looks too high in energy and you mispredict the resting state.

DFT can also screen ligand candidates before synthesis. Calculate ΔG‡ for OA across a library of phosphines; pick the lowest. Calculate ΔΔG‡ between R and S transition states for an asymmetric reaction; predict ee. The energetic span model (Kozuch and Shaik) reduces a full DFT cycle to a single quantity: the largest energy gap between any intermediate and any subsequent transition state along the cycle. That single number is the effective barrier; everything else is detail. The model is now a standard tool for catalyst design.
mathExpressions: \delta E = T_{\text{TDTS}} - I_{\text{TDI}} \quad \text{(energetic span: TDTS = TD transition state, TDI = TD intermediate)}
